newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS-Norwich members reap benefit of debut.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Norwich members reap benefit of debut.

text.p: Nearly three million Norwich Union members received windfalls averaging 1,400 pounds ($2,280) on Monday as the insurance company made a sparkling debut on the London stock market.

A widely expected clamour for Norwich Union shares among institutions after a heavily oversubscribed public offering drove the stock well above the flotation strike price set on Sunday at 290 pence per share.

The flotation, the first by a mutually owned British insurer, valued the group at around six and a half billion pounds, making it Britain's third largest quoted insurance group behind Prudential Corp and Royal & Sun Alliance.
Within minutes of the start of trading, which brought to an end 200 years as a mutual, the price had jumped to 356 pence providing a hefty first day profit for shareholders.
By early afternoon Norwich Union was trading at 331 pence, a rise of 41 pence.
The 107 million shares changing hands made it easily the most actively traded company in the market.
Wilder predictions that the shares might trade as high as four pounds proved unfounded though analysts expect the shares to remain volatile over the coming week.
Speculation that the Labour government may remove tax advantages for pension funds owning equities helped take the early froth out of the shares, as the whole market retreated on the tax concerns.
Analysts put 'fair value' of the stock at between 280 pence and 340 pence, though one suggested that valuations would not look excessively stretched at 380 pence.
Others, however, were more cautious.
"I've long thought the predicted prices of 340 and 350 pence were very high and not sustainable for long," said one.
"The offer pricing took place against a very strong stock market and very strong insurance sector share prices. The market could take the 290 pence price but it wasn't a giveaway."

The gains meant the minimum 300 shares received by 1.8 million with-profits members were worth just under 1,000 pounds with many receiving far more depending on the size and duration of their policies.
Around 1.1 million non-profit policyholders received a flat rate 150 shares worth 500 pounds.
Norwich Union policyholders shared a handout of 1.3 billion free shares as well as the chance to subscribe for more shares at a 25 pence discount to the public offer.
Members applied for nearly four times as many shares as were available in the 2.4 billion pound stock offering while institutions subscribed for a mammoth 10 times the number allocated for them.
Applications were severely scaled back with only those members applying for up to 1,500 pounds worth of shares getting their full allotment.

As with recent demutualising building societies Halifax and Alliance & Leicester, unsatisfied demand among investment institutions, some of whom missed out altogether, was a big factor in the early rise in the stock price.

Like Halifax, Norwich Union is certain to enter the FTSE 100 index of Britain's largest companies later this year, heightening demand among institutions keen to maintain the weighting of the financial sector in their portfolios.
Many of those lucky enough to get shares may decide to cash in immediately especially members borrowing to fund the purchase of extra shares.
With the discount, they are sitting on immediate profits of 66 pence per share, 373 pounds for someone successfully applying for 1,500 pounds worth of shares.

That may help to relieve the upward pressure on the stock price as institutions which hold just over 20 percent of the company seek to make up the shortfalls in their allocations. ($ = 0.612 British Pounds)
